claim: Many animal species employ sperm nuclear basic proteins (SNBPs) or protamines to package sperm genomes tightly.
source: Many animal species employ sperm nuclear basic proteins (SNBPs) or protamines to package sperm genomes tightly.
evidence: This is a general statement about animal biology supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: SNBPs vary across animal lineages and evolve rapidly in mammals.
source: SNBPs vary across animal lineages and evolve rapidly in mammals.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on SNBP evolution in mammals.

claim: Most SNBP genes in Drosophila melanogaster evolve under positive selection except for genes essential for male fertility.
source: We found that most SNBP genes in Drosophila melanogaster evolve under positive selection except for genes essential for male fertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by McDonald-Kreitman tests and dN/dS analyses presented in the manuscript (Table 1, Figure 1).

claim: Evolutionarily young SNBP genes are more likely to be critical for fertility than ancient, conserved SNBP genes.
source: Unexpectedly, evolutionarily young SNBP genes are more likely to be critical for fertility than ancient, conserved SNBP genes.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that Mst77F and Prtl99C are young and essential, while CG30056 is ancient but dispensable.

claim: CG30056 is dispensable for male fertility despite being one of three SNBP genes universally retained in Drosophila species.
source: For example, CG30056 is dispensable for male fertility despite being one of three SNBP genes universally retained in Drosophila species.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR knockout experiments and fertility assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: There were 19 independent SNBP gene amplification events that occurred preferentially on sex chromosomes.
source: We found 19 independent SNBP gene amplification events that occurred preferentially on sex chromosomes.
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis across 78 Drosophila species shown in Figure 3.

claim: The montium group of Drosophila species lost otherwise-conserved SNBP genes, coincident with an X-Y chromosomal fusion.
source: Conversely, the montium group of Drosophila species lost otherwise-conserved SNBP genes, coincident with an X-Y chromosomal fusion.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic analysis and genetic mapping shown in Figure 6.

claim: SNBP genes that became linked to sex chromosomes via chromosomal fusions were more likely to degenerate or relocate back to autosomes.
source: Furthermore, SNBP genes that became linked to sex chromosomes via chromosomal fusions were more likely to degenerate or relocate back to autosomes.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of chromosomal fusions shown in Figure 5.

claim: Autosomal SNBP genes suppress meiotic drive.
source: We hypothesize that autosomal SNBP genes suppress meiotic drive, whereas sex-chromosomal SNBP expansions lead to meiotic drive.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations and prior work on ProtA/ProtB and Segregation Distorter.

claim: Sex-chromosomal SNBP expansions lead to meiotic drive.
source: We hypothesize that autosomal SNBP genes suppress meiotic drive, whereas sex-chromosomal SNBP expansions lead to meiotic drive.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations and prior work on Dox.

claim: X-Y fusions in the montium group render autosomal SNBPs dispensable by making X-versus-Y meiotic drive obsolete or costly.
source: X-Y fusions in the montium group render autosomal SNBPs dispensable by making X-versus-Y meiotic drive obsolete or costly.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the loss of SNBP genes in the montium group.

claim: Genetic conflicts between sex chromosomes may drive SNBP rapid evolution during spermatogenesis in Drosophila species.
source: Thus, genetic conflicts between sex chromosomes may drive SNBP rapid evolution during spermatogenesis in Drosophila species.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the paper, supported by multiple lines of evidence including amplifications, losses, and positive selection.

claim: SNBPs can reduce the size of sperm nuclei by 20–200-fold compared to histone-enriched nuclei.
source: As a result of their tighter DNA packaging, SNBPs can reduce the size of the sperm nuclei by 20–200-fold compared to histone-enriched nuclei (Brewer et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brewer et al., 1999.

claim: Sexual selection for competitive sperm shapes led to the evolutionary origins of SNBP genes in most animal taxa.
source: Based on their role in condensing sperm nuclei, the prevailing hypothesis is that sexual selection for competitive sperm shapes led to the evolutionary origins of SNBP genes in most animal taxa (Lüke et al., 2014; Lüpold et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Mammalian SNBPs in mature sperm include protamine 1 (PRM1) and protamine 2 (PRM2).
source: Mammalian SNBPs in mature sperm include protamine 1 (PRM1) and protamine 2 (PRM2), which are encoded in an autosomal gene cluster that includes Transition Protein 2 (TNP2) and protamine 3 (PRM3) (Martin-Coello et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Martin-Coello et al., 2011.

claim: Both PRM1 and PRM2 are essential for fertility in humans and mice.
source: Both PRM1 and PRM2 are essential for fertility in humans and mice; their expression levels directly affect sperm quality (Balhorn, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Balhorn, 2007.

claim: Loss of PRM1 or PRM2 leads to defects in sperm head morphology and fertility in mice and humans.
source: Loss of PRM1 or PRM2 leads to defects in sperm head morphology and fertility in mice and humans (Cho et al., 2003; Cho et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cho et al., 2003 and Cho et al., 2001.

claim: PRM2 has undergone pseudogenization in bulls.
source: Yet, PRM2 has undergone pseudogenization in bulls (Balhorn, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Balhorn, 2007.

claim: SNBPs were independently derived from different ancestral proteins across taxa.
source: Whereas histones have ancient origins, SNBPs were independently derived from different ancestral proteins across taxa (Eirín-López and Ausió, 2009; Reynolds and Wolfe, 1984; Török and Gornik, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple papers.

claim: SNBPs arose from linker histone H1 gene variants in liverworts and tunicates.
source: For example, SNBPs arose from linker histone H1 gene variants in liverworts and tunicates (Lewis et al., 2004; D'Ippolito et al., 2019), whereas they arose from histone H2B gene variants in cnidarians and echinoderms (Török et al., 2016; Green and Poccia, 1988; Eirín-López et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lewis et al., 2004 and D'Ippolito et al., 2019.

claim: SNBPs arose from histone H2B gene variants in cnidarians and echinoderms.
source: For example, SNBPs arose from linker histone H1 gene variants in liverworts and tunicates (Lewis et al., 2004; D'Ippolito et al., 2019), whereas they arose from histone H2B gene variants in cnidarians and echinoderms (Török et al., 2016; Green and Poccia, 1988; Eirín-López et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Török et al., 2016, Green and Poccia, 1988, and Eirín-López et al., 2006.

claim: PRM1 and PRM2 are among the most rapidly evolving protein-coding genes encoded in mammalian genomes.
source: For example, PRM1 and PRM2 are among the most rapidly evolving protein-coding genes encoded in mammalian genomes (Saperas and Ausió, 2013) and evolve under positive selection in many lineages (Lüke et al., 2014; Wyckoff and Wang, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saperas and Ausió, 2013, Lüke et al., 2014, and Wyckoff and Wang, 2000.

claim: PRM1 and PRM2 evolve under positive selection in many lineages.
source: For example, PRM1 and PRM2 are among the most rapidly evolving protein-coding genes encoded in mammalian genomes (Saperas and Ausió, 2013) and evolve under positive selection in many lineages (Lüke et al., 2014; Wyckoff and Wang, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lüke et al., 2014 and Wyckoff and Wang, 2000.

claim: The arginine content of PRM1 is partially correlated across species with sperm head length.
source: For example, the arginine content of PRM1 is partially correlated across species with sperm head length, which may reflect the selective pressures of sperm competition (Lüke et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lüke et al., 2016b.

claim: Drosophila SNBPs independently arose from proteins encoding high mobility group box (HMG-box) DNA-binding proteins.
source: Previous studies have shown that Drosophila SNBPs independently arose from proteins encoding high mobility group box (HMG-box) DNA-binding proteins (Gärtner et al., 2015); thus, they have distinct origins and likely functions from mammalian protamines.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gärtner et al., 2015.

claim: Five HMG-box SNBP genes have been previously identified in Drosophila melanogaster: ProtA, ProtB, ddbt, Mst77F, and Prtl99C.
source: Five HMG-box SNBP genes have been previously identified in Drosophila melanogaster: ProtA, ProtB, ddbt, Mst77F, and Prtl99C (Tirmarche et al., 2014; Kimura and Loppin, 2016; Jayaramaiah Raja and Renkawitz-Pohl, 2005; Eren-Ghiani et al., 2015; Yamaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple papers.

claim: Each of the five SNBPs is incorporated into nuclei independently of each other.
source: Each of these five SNBPs is incorporated into nuclei independently of each other, suggesting that they play distinct roles in sperm formation (Kimura and Loppin, 2016; Eren-Ghiani et al., 2015; Rathke et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kimura and Loppin, 2016, Eren-Ghiani et al., 2015, and Rathke et al., 2010.

claim: 10 other male-specific proteins with the HMG-box motif were identified in D. melanogaster.
source: Based on the common HMG-box motifs found in these five SNBPs, 10 other male-specific proteins with the same motif were later identified in D. melanogaster (Gärtner et al., 2015; Eren-Ghiani et al., 2015), and 4 of them were later shown to be enriched in sperm nuclei (Gärtner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gärtner et al., 2015 and Eren-Ghiani et al., 2015.

claim: 4 of the 10 male-specific HMG-box proteins were shown to be enriched in sperm nuclei.
source: Based on the common HMG-box motifs found in these five SNBPs, 10 other male-specific proteins with the same motif were later identified in D. melanogaster (Gärtner et al., 2015; Eren-Ghiani et al., 2015), and 4 of them were later shown to be enriched in sperm nuclei (Gärtner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gärtner et al., 2015.

claim: The drive strength of Segregation Distorter can be enhanced by the knockdown of ProtA/ProtB genes.
source: One of the first identified drivers is Segregation Distorter in D. melanogaster, whose drive strength can be further enhanced by the knockdown of ProtA/ProtB genes (Gingell and McLean, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gingell and McLean, 2020.

claim: ProtA/ProtB serve as suppressors of meiotic drive.
source: Thus, ProtA/ProtB serve as suppressors of meiotic drive through an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that knockdown of ProtA/ProtB enhances Segregation Distorter drive.

claim: Dox emerged via the stepwise acquisition of multiple gene segments, mostly from ProtA/ProtB.
source: Dox emerged via the stepwise acquisition of multiple gene segments, mostly from ProtA/ProtB.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tao et al., 2007a.

claim: Dox produces chromosome condensation defects in Y chromosome-containing sperm during spermatogenesis.
source: Dox produces chromosome condensation defects in Y chromosome-containing sperm during spermatogenesis, ultimately leading to X-chromosomal bias among functional sperm and sex-ratio bias in resulting progeny (Tao et al., 2007a; Faulhaber, 1967; Tao et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tao et al., 2007a, Faulhaber, 1967, and Tao et al., 2007b.

claim: Dox-like genes have amplified and diversified on the X chromosome in D. simulans and sister species.
source: In D. simulans and sister species, Dox-like genes have amplified and diversified on the X chromosome in an escalating battle between X and Y chromosomes for transmission through the male germline (Vedanayagam et al., 2021; Muirhead and Presgraves, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vedanayagam et al., 2021 and Muirhead and Presgraves, 2021.

claim: 15 autosomal SNBP genes function at different stages of spermatogenesis in D. melanogaster.
source: Our survey did not reveal any additional genes beyond the 15 previously identified autosomal SNBP genes, which function at different stages of spermatogenesis (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on a survey of testis-specific genes encoding HMG boxes and prior literature.

claim: CG14835, ProtA, ProtB, Mst77F, Prtl99C, and ddbt all encode SNBP proteins present in the mature sperm head.
source: For example, CG14835, ProtA, ProtB, Mst77F, Prtl99C, and ddbt all encode SNBP proteins present in the mature sperm head (Jayaramaiah Raja and Renkawitz-Pohl, 2005; Eren-Ghiani et al., 2015; Yamaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple papers.

claim: Tpl94D, tHMG-1, tHMG-2, and CG30356 encode transition SNBP proteins during the transition between histone and protamines but are not retained in mature sperm.
source: In contrast, Tpl94D, tHMG-1, tHMG-2, and CG30356 encode transition SNBP proteins during the transition between histone and protamines but are not retained in mature sperm (Gärtner et al., 2015; Rathke et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gärtner et al., 2015 and Rathke et al., 2007.

claim: All candidate SNBP genes are transcribed in male germline cells, with the highest level of expression of most SNBP genes occurring in late spermatocytes.
source: Using single-cell transcriptomic data (Witt et al., 2021), we confirmed that all candidate SNBP genes are transcribed in male germline cells, with the highest level of expression of most SNBP genes occurring in late spermatocytes.
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell transcriptomic data from Witt et al., 2021.

claim: CG34269 is transcribed earlier in late spermatogonia.
source: The only exceptions are CG34269, which is transcribed earlier in late spermatogonia, and CG30056, which is transcribed later in late spermatids (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CG30056 is transcribed later in late spermatids.
source: The only exceptions are CG34269, which is transcribed earlier in late spermatogonia, and CG30056, which is transcribed later in late spermatids (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: SNBP proteins in D. melanogaster tend to be short (<200 a.a.) and mostly have high isoelectric points (>10).
source: SNBP proteins in D. melanogaster tend to be short (<200 a.a.) and mostly have high isoelectric points (>10), consistent with their basic charge and potential function in tight packaging of DNA (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of SNBP protein properties shown in Table 1.

claim: 11 SNBP genes encode a single HMG box, whereas four genes (Tpl94D, Prtl99C, Mst33A, and CG42355) encode two HMG boxes.
source: A closer examination revealed that 11 SNBP genes encode a single HMG box, whereas four genes (Tpl94D, Prtl99C, Mst33A, and CG42355) encode two HMG boxes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of SNBP gene structures shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: tHMG and Prot underwent recent gene duplications in D. melanogaster.
source: Our phylogenomic analyses revealed that two SNBP genes (tHMG and Prot) underwent recent gene duplications in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: tHMG-1 and tHMG-2, ProtA and ProtB are present as closely related paralogs in D. melanogaster but only in one copy in closely related species.
source: Both are present as closely related paralogs (tHMG-1 and tHMG-2, ProtA and ProtB) in D. melanogaster but only in one copy in closely related species (Figure 1; Tirmarche et al., 2014; Jayaramaiah Raja and Renkawitz-Pohl, 2005).
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 1 and citations to prior work.

claim: Five SNBP genes are found only in the Sophophora subgenus: CG42355, Mst33A, Mst77F, Prtl99C, and Tpl94D.
source: Five SNBP genes are found only in the Sophophora subgenus: CG42355, Mst33A, Mst77F, Prtl99C, and Tpl94D (Figure 1), and are, therefore, less than 40 million years old.
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Eight D. melanogaster SNBP genes (CG14835, CG30056, CG30356, CG31010, CG34529, ddbt, tHMG, and Prot) have orthologs in the outgroup species, S. lebanonensis.
source: At the other extreme, we found orthologs of eight D. melanogaster SNBP genes (CG14835, CG30056, CG30356, CG31010, CG34529, ddbt, tHMG, and Prot) in the outgroup species, S. lebanonensis.
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Eight SNBP genes are at least 50 million years old.
source: Thus, these eight SNBP genes are at least 50 million years old (Suvorov et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis and a citation to Suvorov et al., 2022 for divergence time.

claim: 11 of 13 SNBP genes (except CG30056 and ProtA) evolve faster (higher dN/dS) than 95% of protein-coding genes across the genome.
source: We found that 11 of 13 SNBP genes (except CG30056 and ProtA) evolve faster (higher dN/dS) than 95% of protein-coding genes across the genome (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on dN/dS analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: High protein evolution rates of SNBP genes are due to high dN instead of low dS.
source: These high protein evolution rates are due to high dN instead of low dS (Figure 1C), suggesting that SNBPs evolve under either extensive positive selection or reduced functional constraints.
evidence: This is based on dN analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Five SNBP genes in D. melanogaster have evolved under positive selection during its divergence from D. simulans.
source: Indeed, our tests reveal that five SNBP genes in D. melanogaster have evolved under positive selection during its divergence from D. simulans (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on McDonald-Kreitman tests shown in Table 1.

claim: tHMG-1, but not its paralog, tHMG-2, evolved under positive selection in D. melanogaster.
source: By polarizing the test using the inferred ancestral sequences of tHMG-1 and tHMG-2, we find that tHMG-1, but not its paralog, tHMG-2, evolved under positive selection in D. melanogaster (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on polarized McDonald-Kreitman tests shown in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Four genes (CG30356, CG31010, CG42355, Tpl94D) evolved under positive selection in both D. melanogaster and D. serrata.
source: Among the SNBP genes shared between D. melanogaster and D. serrata, we found that four genes (CG30356, CG31010, CG42355, Tpl94D) evolved under positive selection in both D. melanogaster and D. serrata, whereas two genes (CG30056, ddbt) do not show a signature of positive selection in either species (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on McDonald-Kreitman tests in both species shown in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Two genes (CG30056, ddbt) do not show a signature of positive selection in either D. melanogaster or D. serrata.
source: Among the SNBP genes shared between D. melanogaster and D. serrata, we found that four genes (CG30356, CG31010, CG42355, Tpl94D) evolved under positive selection in both D. melanogaster and D. serrata, whereas two genes (CG30056, ddbt) do not show a signature of positive selection in either species (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on McDonald-Kreitman tests in both species shown in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Three additional genes (CG34269 and two ProtA/B duplicates) evolved under positive selection only in D. serrata.
source: Three additional genes (CG34269 and two ProtA/B duplicates) evolved under positive selection only in D. serrata (ProtA/B underwent independent gene duplications in D. melanogaster and D. serrata).
evidence: This is based on McDonald-Kreitman tests shown in Table 1 and Supplementary file 5.

claim: ProtA/B underwent independent gene duplications in D. melanogaster and D. serrata.
source: Three additional genes (CG34269 and two ProtA/B duplicates) evolved under positive selection only in D. serrata (ProtA/B underwent independent gene duplications in D. melanogaster and D. serrata).
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis.

claim: Three genes (Mst77F, Prtl99C, and ddbt) are essential for male fertility in D. melanogaster.
source: Three genes (Mst77F, Prtl99C, and ddbt) are essential for male fertility (Tirmarche et al., 2014; Kimura and Loppin, 2016; Jayaramaiah Raja and Renkawitz-Pohl, 2005; Eren-Ghiani et al., 2015; Rathke et al., 2010), but separate knockouts of six individual genes (CG14835, ProtA, ProtB Tpl94D, tHMG-1, and tHMG-2) do not appear to impair male fertility under standard laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is based on prior knockout/knockdown experiments cited in the text.

claim: Separate knockouts of six individual genes (CG14835, ProtA, ProtB Tpl94D, tHMG-1, and tHMG-2) do not appear to impair male fertility under standard laboratory conditions.
source: Three genes (Mst77F, Prtl99C, and ddbt) are essential for male fertility (Tirmarche et al., 2014; Kimura and Loppin, 2016; Jayaramaiah Raja and Renkawitz-Pohl, 2005; Eren-Ghiani et al., 2015; Rathke et al., 2010), but separate knockouts of six individual genes (CG14835, ProtA, ProtB Tpl94D, tHMG-1, and tHMG-2) do not appear to impair male fertility under standard laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is based on prior knockout/knockdown experiments cited in the text.

claim: Double knockouts of ProtA/ProtB show a fertility cost only in conditions of sperm exhaustion via mating with excess numbers of females.
source: Further experimentation has revealed a fertility cost for double knockouts of ProtA/ProtB but only in conditions of sperm exhaustion via mating with excess numbers of females (Tirmarche et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Tirmarche et al., 2014.

claim: Proteins essential for male fertility (Mst77F, Prtl99C, and ddbt) are more likely to be present in the mature sperm head.
source: Instead, proteins essential for male fertility (Mst77F, Prtl99C, and ddbt) are more likely to be present in the mature sperm head, whereas transition SNBPs (Tpl94D, tHMG-1, and tHMG-2) are more likely to be dispensable, potentially due to functional redundancy with each other.
evidence: This is based on comparison of protein localization and essentiality data.

claim: Transition SNBPs (Tpl94D, tHMG-1, and tHMG-2) are more likely to be dispensable, potentially due to functional redundancy with each other.
source: Instead, proteins essential for male fertility (Mst77F, Prtl99C, and ddbt) are more likely to be present in the mature sperm head, whereas transition SNBPs (Tpl94D, tHMG-1, and tHMG-2) are more likely to be dispensable, potentially due to functional redundancy with each other.
evidence: This is based on comparison of protein localization and essentiality data, with speculation about redundancy.

claim: SNBP genes important for male fertility in D. melanogaster show no signature of positive selection according to McDonald–Kreitman tests.
source: Moreover, SNBP genes important for male fertility in D. melanogaster show no signature of positive selection according to McDonald–Kreitman tests.
evidence: This is based on McDonald-Kreitman tests shown in Table 1.

claim: Two of the three identified transition SNBP genes evolve under positive selection (Tpl94D and tHMG-1).
source: In contrast, two of the three identified transition SNBP genes evolve under positive selection (Tpl94D and tHMG-1).
evidence: This is based on McDonald-Kreitman tests shown in Table 1.

claim: Two essential SNBP genes (Prtl99C and Mst77F) are evolutionarily young.
source: We find that two essential SNBP genes (Prtl99C and Mst77F) are evolutionarily young, i.e., they arose relatively recently in Drosophila evolution.
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Prtl99C and Mst77F have been lost at least once in the montium group species since their birth.
source: Moreover, both genes have been lost at least once in the montium group species since their birth.
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: ddbt arose before the separation of Drosophila and S. lebanonensis.
source: The third essential SNBP gene, ddbt, arose before the separation of Drosophila and S. lebanonensis, but it has also been lost at least once (in D. willistoni) among the 15 species analyzed (Yamaki et al., 2016 Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: ddbt has been lost at least once (in D. willistoni) among the 15 species analyzed.
source: The third essential SNBP gene, ddbt, arose before the separation of Drosophila and S. lebanonensis, but it has also been lost at least once (in D. willistoni) among the 15 species analyzed (Yamaki et al., 2016 Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Only two SNBP genes have been strictly retained across all Drosophila species — Prot and CG30056.
source: Based on this analysis, we find only two SNBP genes have been strictly retained across all Drosophila species — Prot and CG30056 (Figure 1A), while the CG31010 gene has only been lost in one species.
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis across 78 Drosophila species.

claim: CG31010 gene has only been lost in one species.
source: Based on this analysis, we find only two SNBP genes have been strictly retained across all Drosophila species — Prot and CG30056 (Figure 1A), while the CG31010 gene has only been lost in one species.
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis across 78 Drosophila species.

claim: Prot and CG30056 have the lowest dN/dS among SNBP genes.
source: Prot and CG30056 also have the lowest dN/dS among SNBP genes (Figure 1B), suggesting that they evolve under a higher degree of selective constraint than other SNBP genes.
evidence: This is based on dN/dS analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A dual loss of ProtA/ProtB reduces male fertility in conditions of sperm exhaustion in D. melanogaster.
source: Previous studies have shown that a dual loss of ProtA/ProtB reduces male fertility in conditions of sperm exhaustion in D. melanogaster (Tirmarche et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Tirmarche et al., 2014.

claim: CG30056 is located in an intron of frazzled, a gene essential for development and morphogenesis.
source: CG30056 is located in an intron of frazzled, a gene essential for development and morphogenesis (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Homozygous CG30056 knockout flies were viable.
source: Homozygous knockout flies were viable, confirming that the removal of CG30056 did not disrupt the essential frazzled gene.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation of knockout flies.

claim: Loss of CG30056 does not significantly lower male fertility.
source: We found only modest differences in offspring number between heterozygous controls and homozygous knockout males (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 8), implying that loss of CG30056 does not significantly lower male fertility.
evidence: This is based on fertility assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No evidence of sex-ratio distortion was detected in crosses with CG30056 knockout males.
source: We also detected no evidence of sex-ratio distortion in our crosses (Figure 2C; Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is based on sex-ratio analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Parallel fertility experiments with Mst77F mutants confirmed the essentiality of Mst77F.
source: Parallel fertility experiments conducted with mutants of Mst77F or Tpl94D recapitulated previous findings, confirming the essentiality of Mst77F and the dispensability of Tpl94D (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 8; Gärtner et al., 2015; Kimura and Loppin, 2016).
evidence: This is based on fertility assays shown in Figure 2B and citations to prior work.

claim: Parallel fertility experiments with Tpl94D mutants confirmed the dispensability of Tpl94D.
source: Parallel fertility experiments conducted with mutants of Mst77F or Tpl94D recapitulated previous findings, confirming the essentiality of Mst77F and the dispensability of Tpl94D (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 8; Gärtner et al., 2015; Kimura and Loppin, 2016).
evidence: This is based on fertility assays shown in Figure 2B and citations to prior work.

claim: No significant fertility difference was found between CG30056-KO and control sibling males in sperm exhaustion experiments.
source: In spite of this increased stringency, we did not find a significant fertility difference between CG30056-KO and the control sibling males (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on sperm exhaustion fertility assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 8 of 13 D. melanogaster SNBP genes investigated (CG14835, ddbt, Mst33A, Mst77F, Prtl99C, Prot, tHMG, and CG31010) underwent amplification in at least one species.
source: We found that 8 of 13 D. melanogaster SNBP genes investigated (CG14835, ddbt, Mst33A, Mst77F, Prtl99C, Prot, tHMG, and CG31010) underwent amplification in at least one species (Figure 3 and Table 2).
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis across 78 Drosophila species shown in Figure 3.

claim: SNBP genes have experienced 20 independent amplification events.
source: In total, we found that SNBP genes have experienced 20 independent amplification events, including one event in the outgroup species, Leucophenga varia (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Most SNBP amplifications are evolutionarily young (<10 million years old).
source: Most SNBP amplifications are evolutionarily young (<10 million years old; Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and 15 of them are specific to a single surveyed species (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: 15 SNBP amplifications are specific to a single surveyed species.
source: Most SNBP amplifications are evolutionarily young (<10 million years old; Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and 15 of them are specific to a single surveyed species (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Most amplified copies encode positively charged HMG domain-containing proteins.
source: Like their parental genes, most amplified copies encode positively charged HMG domain-containing proteins (Supplementary file 3) and have male-specific, mostly testis-specific, expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of protein properties and expression data.

claim: Amplified copies have male-specific, mostly testis-specific, expression.
source: Like their parental genes, most amplified copies encode positively charged HMG domain-containing proteins (Supplementary file 3) and have male-specific, mostly testis-specific, expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Many amplified SNBP genes are arranged in tandem arrays.
source: Many amplified SNBP genes are arranged in tandem arrays, making their sequences hard to assemble.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of amplified SNBP genes.

claim: Eight amplifications are X-linked and four are Y-linked.
source: We found that eight amplifications are X-linked and four are Y-linked, whereas, for four amplifications, we can infer sex chromosomal linkage but cannot distinguish between X- or Y-linkage (Figure 3; Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is based on chromosomal assignment analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: 80% (16/20) of amplifications occurred on sex chromosomes.
source: Thus, we conclude that 80% (16/20, Figure 3B) of amplifications occurred on sex chromosomes.
evidence: This is based on counting amplifications on sex chromosomes shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The high fraction of sex chromosomal amplifications is significantly higher than the null expectation.
source: This high fraction is significantly higher than the null expectation (Test of Proportions, p=2.3e-5) if SNBP amplifications were randomly distributed between sex chromosomes or autosomes.
evidence: This is based on statistical test of proportions.

claim: tHMG copies on the heterochromatic X chromosome (tHMG-hetX) experienced two duplications before the amplification.
source: From these analyses, we inferred that tHMG copies on the heterochromatic X chromosome (tHMG-hetX) experienced two duplications before the amplification.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and synteny analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: tHMG-hetX evolves considerably faster than tHMG-Anc.
source: Within an 81 amino acid residue stretch, we found 19 non-synonymous changes that occurred within tHMG-hetX compared to just 4 non-synonymous changes that occurred within tHMG-Anc (Figure 4B). Thus, tHMG-hetX evolves considerably faster than tHMG-Anc.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both tHMG-hetX and tHMG-Anc branches have significantly higher protein evolution rates than branches in other species.
source: Branch analyses using PAML revealed that both tHMG-hetX and tHMG-Anc branches have significantly higher protein evolution rates than branches in other species (Figure 4C; ω = 1.6, LRT test, p=0.007; Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is based on PAML branch analysis shown in Figure 4C and Supplementary file 11.

claim: The montium group of Drosophila species suffered a precipitous loss of at least five SNBP genes.
source: Our phylogenomic analyses also highlighted one Drosophila clade—the montium group of species (including D. kikkawai)—which suffered a precipitous loss of at least five SNBP genes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Six different SNBP genes underwent 11 independent degeneration events in the montium group.
source: A closer examination allowed us to infer that six different SNBP genes underwent 11 independent degeneration events in the montium group (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Five of six SNBP genes lost in the montium clade (Mst77F, Prtl99C, Mst33A, tHMG, CG14835) are also among the eight SNBP genes subject to sex chromosome-specific amplifications in other Drosophila species.
source: Intriguingly, five of six SNBP genes lost in the montium clade (Mst77F, Prtl99C, Mst33A, tHMG, CG14835) are also among the eight SNBP genes subject to sex chromosome-specific amplifications in other Drosophila species (Figure 3 and Table 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of data in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: No SNBP amplification events were found in any species of the montium clade.
source: Notably, we did not find SNBP amplification events in any species of the montium clade.
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Many ancestrally Y-linked genes are present in females in the montium group because of possible relocation to other chromosomes.
source: An important clue came from a previous study, which showed that many ancestrally Y-linked genes are present in females because of possible relocation to other chromosomes in the montium group (Dupim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Dupim et al., 2018.

claim: Most ancestrally Y-linked genes are actually linked to the X chromosome in the montium group.
source: Using the available assemblies with Illumina-based chromosome assignment, we surprisingly found that most ancestrally Y-linked genes are actually linked to the X chromosome (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on chromosomal assignment analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In D. triauraria, 11 of 12 ancestrally Y-linked genes are located on the same region of the X chromosome.
source: Moreover, in D. triauraria, we found that 11 of 12 ancestrally Y-linked genes, i.e., all except JYalpha, are located on the same region of the X chromosome (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A single translocation fused most of the Y chromosome to the X chromosome in the ancestor of the montium group of species.
source: The most parsimonious explanation for these findings is a single translocation fused most of the Y chromosome to the X chromosome in the ancestor of the montium group of species.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most Y-linked genes are on the X chromosome in montium species.

claim: Montium group species still harbor a Y chromosome, but their Y chromosome is missing most ancestrally Y-linked genes.
source: Although montium group species still harbor a Y chromosome, their Y chromosome is missing most ancestrally Y-linked genes.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Some Y-linked genes, e.g., PRY, relocated back to the Y chromosome in some species after the X-Y fusion.
source: After this ancient X-Y chromosomal fusion, some Y-linked genes, e.g., PRY, relocated back to the Y chromosome in some species (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: All F1 males inherit alleles of ancestral Y-linked genes from their mother in D. triauraria.
source: In contrast to these expectations, all F1 males inherit alleles of ancestral Y-linked genes from their mother, unambiguously indicating their X-chromosomal linkage (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on genetic crosses shown in Figure 6C.

claim: X-Y fusion is an extremely rare evolutionary event that has only previously been documented in one vole species.
source: Our finding of an X-Y fusion via both computational and genetic linkage analyses is remarkable because X-Y fusion is an extremely rare evolutionary event that has only previously been documented in one vole species (Couger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Couger et al., 2021.

claim: No meiotic drive has been documented in the montium species.
source: Indeed, no meiotic drive has been documented in the montium species (Courret et al., 2019), although this absence could simply reflect the inadequate number of studies for meiotic drive.
evidence: This is based on a citation to Courret et al., 2019.

claim: In D. melanogaster, most SNBP genes are transcribed before meiosis but translated after meiosis.
source: In D. melanogaster, most SNBP genes are transcribed before meiosis but translated after meiosis (Jayaramaiah Raja and Renkawitz-Pohl, 2005; Rathke et al., 2007; Barckmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on citations to multiple papers.

claim: SNBP transcripts from a single allele can be inherited and translated by all sperm, regardless of which chromosomes they carry.
source: Thus, SNBP transcripts from a single allele, e.g., an X-linked allele, can be inherited and translated by all sperm, regardless of which chromosomes they carry.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of SNBP transcription and translation.

claim: Mammalian SNBPs are only expressed post-meiosis.
source: In contrast, mammalian SNBPs are only expressed post-meiosis (Hecht et al., 1986; Peschon et al., 1987) and, therefore, individual SNBP alleles can only affect the chromatin states of sperm in which they reside.
evidence: This is based on citations to Hecht et al., 1986 and Peschon et al., 1987.

claim: Wolbachia produces toxins that prevent the deposition of SNBP during spermatogenesis.
source: Recent studies have revealed that Wolbachia produces toxins that prevent the deposition of SNBP during spermatogenesis (Kaur et al., 2022) and delay SNBP removal in embryos post-fertilization to accomplish this cytoplasmic incompatibility (Beckmann et al., 2019; Landmann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on citations to Kaur et al., 2022, Beckmann et al., 2019, and Landmann et al., 2009.

claim: Deletions of ProtA/ProtB exacerbate the intensity of cytoplasmic incompatibility imposed by Wolbachia in D. melanogaster.
source: Indeed, deletions of ProtA/ProtB exacerbate the intensity of cytoplasmic incompatibility imposed by Wolbachia in D. melanogaster (Kaur et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Kaur et al., 2022.

claim: The atlas SNBP gene from D. melanogaster does not encode an HMG domain entirely and has arisen de novo.
source: Indeed, recent findings have shown that the atlas SNBP gene from D. melanogaster does not encode an HMG domain entirely and has arisen de novo (Rivard et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Rivard et al., 2021.

claim: ddbt is a conserved SNBP gene with essential sperm telomere-capping function in D. melanogaster.
source: For example, ddbt is a conserved SNBP gene with essential sperm telomere-capping function in D. melanogaster; loss of ddbt leads to defects in telomere capping and induction of telomeric fusions in embryos (Yamaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Yamaki et al., 2016.

claim: Loss of ddbt leads to defects in telomere capping and induction of telomeric fusions in embryos.
source: For example, ddbt is a conserved SNBP gene with essential sperm telomere-capping function in D. melanogaster; loss of ddbt leads to defects in telomere capping and induction of telomeric fusions in embryos (Yamaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Yamaki et al., 2016.

claim: The two lineages that lost ddbt—all D. willistoni subgroup species, and D. albomicans in the D. immigrans species group—have a pair of neo-sex chromosomes due to the fusion of Muller element D and sex chromosomes.
source: We find that the two lineages that lost ddbt—all D. willistoni subgroup species, and D. albomicans in the D. immigrans species group—have a pair of neo-sex chromosomes due to the fusion of Muller element D and sex chromosomes (Sturtevant and Novitski, 1941; Chang et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2012; Ellison and Bachtrog, 2019).
evidence: This is based on citations to multiple papers.

claim: Three SNBP genes that became linked to sex chromosomes via chromosomal fusions either degenerated or translocated back to autosomes.
source: In other lineages, three SNBP genes that became linked to sex chromosomes via chromosomal fusions either degenerated or translocated back to autosomes (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Some newly X-linked SNBP genes either degenerated (two instances out of eight) or translocated back to autosomes (one instance out of eight).
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, some newly X-linked SNBP genes either degenerated (two instances out of eight) or translocated back to autosomes (one instance out of eight).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: In five cases, SNBP genes were still retained on sex chromosomes.
source: In five cases, SNBP genes were still retained on sex chromosomes (Figure 5; Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: ddbt amplified to six copies in D. repletoides.
source: Among these five cases, we observed one amplification event –ddbt amplified to six copies in D. repletoides (Figure 3B), consistent with the idea that it may act as a meiotic driver.
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No instances of pseudogenization or subsequent translocation to the X chromosome of SNBP genes that are still preserved on their original autosomal locations or involved in chromosome fusions between autosomes were found (0/16).
source: In contrast, we found no instances of pseudogenization or subsequent translocation to the X chromosome of SNBP genes that are still preserved on their original autosomal locations or involved in chromosome fusions between autosomes (0/16).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 5 and Supplementary file 12.

claim: The difference in retention patterns between sex chromosomes and autosomes is highly significant (3:5 versus 0:16, Fisher's exact test, p=0.03).
source: This difference is highly significant (Figure 5; Supplementary file 12; 3:5 versus 0:16, Fisher's exact test, p=0.03).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Most SNBP genes are small (<200 amino acids) and positively charged.
source: Like histones, most SNBPs are small (<200 amino acids) and positively charged.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about SNBP protein properties.

claim: Many SNBPs contain a high proportion of lysine, arginine, and cysteine residues.
source: Many SNBPs also contain a high proportion of lysine, arginine, and cysteine residues, which form disulfide bridges to further condense DNA within sperm heads (Török et al., 2016; Eirín-López and Ausió, 2009).
evidence: This is based on citations to Török et al., 2016 and Eirín-López and Ausió, 2009.

claim: 11 of 13 SNBP genes (except CG30056 and ProtA) evolve faster than 95% of protein-coding genes across the genome.
source: We found that 11 of 13 SNBP genes (except CG30056 and ProtA) evolve faster (higher dN/dS) than 95% of protein-coding genes across the genome (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on dN/dS analysis comparing SNBP genes to genome-wide distribution shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Most mammals share four SNBP genes: TNP1, TNP2, PRM1, and PRM2.
source: Most mammals share four SNBP genes: TNP1, TNP2, PRM1, and PRM2.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about mammalian SNBP genes.

claim: SNBP repertoires vary extensively between Drosophila species, with both dramatic gains and losses.
source: In contrast, SNBP repertoires vary extensively between Drosophila species, with both dramatic gains and losses.
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 1 and Figure 3.

claim: Several independent, species-specific amplifications of SNBP genes from 5 to >50 copies preferentially occurred on sex chromosomes.
source: We discovered several independent, species-specific amplifications of SNBP genes from 5 to >50 copies that preferentially occurred on sex chromosomes (Figure 3 and Table 2).
evidence: This is based on phylogenomic analysis shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.
